Something is trite when it has been said, done, or expressed so many times that it has completely lost its freshness, power, and meaning. It once had impact. It once felt real and meaningful. But because people repeated it over and over again — in conversations, books, movies, speeches — it became hollow, bland, and boring. When you encounter something trite, your brain barely registers it. It slides right off, like water off glass.

The single most important idea to hold on to: trite things are worn out from overuse.
A Simple Way to See It

Imagine a brand new joke. The first time you hear it, you laugh. The second time, you smile. The fifth time, you groan. The fiftieth time, you feel absolutely nothing. That joke has become trite. It hasn't changed — but exposure has drained every drop of life from it.

Now apply that same idea to phrases, advice, ideas, and even storylines in movies. That's where "trite" lives.

Trite phrases in everyday speech:

  • "Everything happens for a reason."
  • "Follow your dreams."
  • "At the end of the day..."
  • "Time heals all wounds."
  • "Be yourself."

These weren't always trite. At some point in history, someone said one of these things and it genuinely moved people. It felt wise and true. But they got repeated millions of times — in greeting cards, in motivational posters, in speeches — until they became verbal wallpaper. Today, when someone says "time heals all wounds" to comfort a grieving person, it often feels lazy and empty rather than warm and helpful. That's trite.

Trite ideas in storytelling:

A movie where the underdog sports team, after many struggles, wins the championship in the final seconds through the power of friendship and belief — you've seen this a hundred times. A villain who is evil just because he's the villain, with no real depth or reason. A love story where two people hate each other at first and then fall in love. These story ideas are trite. They're not necessarily bad ideas, but they've been done so many times, without any fresh angle, that they feel predictable and unimaginative.
Why "Trite" is Always a Negative Word

Trite is never a compliment. Calling something trite is a polite but sharp criticism. It says: this is lazy thinking. It suggests the person didn't bother to find a new, honest, or thoughtful way to express something. They just reached for the nearest ready-made phrase or idea on the shelf and used it without thinking.

When a writer is told their work is trite, it stings — because it means they haven't brought anything original to the table. They've served up leftovers.
A Crucial Nuance: Trite Does Not Mean False

This is important. Something can be trite and still be completely true.

"Hard work pays off" — this may well be true. But it is also trite, because it has been said so endlessly, in so many predictable situations, that it no longer makes anyone stop and think. It has lost the ability to carry real weight, even when the underlying truth is valid.

So trite is not about whether something is right or wrong. It's about whether it has any freshness or life left in it.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Understanding "trite" gets sharper when you compare it to words that are close in meaning.

Cliché is the closest cousin to trite. In fact, they're nearly interchangeable in most situations. However, "cliché" is most often used specifically for overused phrases and expressions, while "trite" can describe phrases, ideas, plots, arguments, or any form of expression that feels stale from overuse. You'd more naturally say a phrase is a cliché, but an entire story idea, argument, or piece of art is trite (though "cliché" is often used for these too in everyday conversation).

Hackneyed means essentially the same thing as trite — worn out from being used too much. It's a bit more formal and old-fashioned sounding. If you know "trite," you essentially know "hackneyed."

Banal means lacking any originality or depth — dull and uninteresting. Banal is slightly broader than trite. A thing can be banal simply because it's dull by nature, without necessarily being overused. Trite, on the other hand, specifically implies it used to have value that has been worn away.

Platitude is a noun — it refers to a specific trite remark, especially one delivered as if it were profound wisdom. When someone tries to comfort you after a loss and says "God only gives you what you can handle," that is a platitude. The adjective form of platitude is "platitudinous," which means the same thing as trite.

Seeing a word in action is one of the best ways to lock in its meaning.

  • "The graduation speech was full of trite advice about believing in yourself and chasing your dreams — nothing the students hadn't heard a hundred times before."
  • "The film's ending felt trite and predictable; every beat was something you could see coming from a mile away."
  • "She wanted to say something comforting, but everything that came to mind felt trite, so she simply sat quietly beside him."
  • "Critics dismissed the novel as trite, arguing that its themes of good versus evil were handled with no originality whatsoever."
  • "His essay was well-written in terms of grammar, but the ideas were trite — he had nothing new to say."

The opposites of trite are words like fresh, original, novel, insightful, striking, and profound. A fresh observation is one that makes you pause and think: I've never quite thought of it that way before. A profound idea has genuine depth and moves you. These are the things trite is not.

Whenever you want to know if something is trite, ask yourself two questions:

1. Have I heard or seen this many, many times before?
2. Does it feel like someone said it without really thinking?

If the answer to both is yes, it's almost certainly trite.

Trite is the word you use when something that should feel meaningful has been repeated so often it has gone completely flat. It is a word that lives in the world of language, ideas, art, and expression. It carries a quiet but definite sting — it accuses something of being unoriginal, thoughtless, and empty. Great writers, speakers, and thinkers work hard to avoid being trite, always searching for the fresher, truer, more honest way to say something.
